title: Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu
hook: Nanak's mother loved him gently; his father, an accountant, worried for his future

segments.voice: Yesterday, sant: a weaver beside a king, a Sufi beside a shoemaker. Your line was room for all. Did you pull out a chair for someone? Day eight hundred two.

A father counts out coins into his son's hand. Go to the market, he says. Buy well, sell well, come home with a profit. Show me you can make your way. The son comes home with empty hands and no goods. On the road, he says, he met holy men who hadn't eaten, and he fed them. That, he says, was the true bargain. The father is furious. The mother, as tradition remembers her, is gentler. A new part of the path begins today: the people around the Gurus. And it starts at home, with Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu.
screen: `COINS FOR THE MARKET.` → `EMPTY HANDS, FED STRANGERS.` → `A NEW PART: THE PEOPLE AROUND THE GURUS.`

segments.voice: The story of the coins isn't in the Granth. It comes from the janamsakhis, the old life-stories of Guru Nanak, and Sikhs remember it as the sacha sauda, the true bargain. The janamsakhis give us his parents in a few strokes. His father, Mehta Kalu, kept the village accounts, a practical man with a practical hope: that his son would find steady work and get on in the world. His mother, Mata Tripta, the stories remember as gentle, the one who loved the boy as he was. Here's what's worth noticing. The stories don't make Mehta Kalu a villain. A father worried about money and a future is not a bad man. He's a father. In one story, the boy grows quiet and withdrawn, lying for days without wanting to eat, and the family, worried, calls in a physician. And here the Granth itself has a line. In a salok in Raag Malar, on Ang 1279, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: they called the physician to treat me; he took my arm and felt for the illness; the simple physician doesn't know the pain is deep inside, in the heart. Whether that salok was spoken in that very room, the sources don't settle. But it fits. The family's worry was real, and so was their love. They just couldn't see where the ache was. That's the picture of this home. A mother's gentleness. A father's worry. Neither of them fully understood their son, and both of them loved him. Love and worry live in the same house, at the same table, often in the same parent.
screen: `THE TRUE BARGAIN: A JANAMSAKHI STORY.` · `A FATHER WHO KEPT ACCOUNTS.` · `A PHYSICIAN WHO MISSED THE ACHE.` · `GENTLENESS AND WORRY, BOTH LOVE.` · then, large: `LOVE AND WORRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a parent's worry. In the sit, bring to mind someone who worried about you: a parent, a grandparent, a guardian, an older friend. Remember one thing they worried over, maybe something that annoyed you at the time. Then look underneath it for the love that was holding it. You don't have to agree with the worry. Just see what it was made of. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mata. A title of honor for the Gurus' mothers and wives: Guru Nanak's mother, gentle, her husband worried, and love and worry living in the same home.
Your line: love and worry. Today, if you can, tell someone who worried about you that you know it came from love, or simply say thank you for it in your own heart. Day eight hundred two.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the stories of Guru Nanak's childhood from the janamsakhis, especially at Gurpurab, and the sacha sauda, the true bargain, is among the stories children hear at home and in gurdwara classes.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strict father and a soft mother.
what it means: a home where gentleness and worry were both forms of love for a son they didn't fully understand.
what a scholar hears: the family details come from the janamsakhis, while the physician salok on Ang 1279 is Guru Nanak's own, and the sources don't settle when it was spoken.
recall: a bard, a poet of praise

notes: Paraphrase of the salok 'vaid bulaia vaidagi pakarh dhandholae baanh; bhola vaid na jaanee karak kaleje maahi' (Malar ki Var, Ang 1279): confirm ang and paraphrase. Script renders kaleja as 'the mind'; a Keeper may prefer 'the heart' or 'deep inside'.
Linking that salok to the janamsakhi physician episode is a traditional association; the script says the sources don't settle it.
Mehta Kalu as the village accountant (patwari) and Mata Tripta as gentle: from janamsakhi tradition; confirm.
The sacha sauda: the script leaves out details that vary between versions (place, amount, whether Kalu struck him).
howItsDone mentions Gurpurab and gurdwara classes generally: confirm.
